newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels take Zaire's diamond capital-mining sources.
newsitem.headline: Rebels take Zaire's diamond capital-mining sources.

text.p: Zairean rebels marched into the diamond-mining capital of Mbuji-Mayi on Friday, adding a jewel to their necklace of victories, mining sources said.
"We understand rebel forces have entered the town. It is in the process of changing sides," said one source who had been in radio contact with the city.
As in many previous takeovers, there were no reports of fighting although much shooting was heard overnight.
Traders in Zaire's second city Lubumbashi, itself targeted by the rebels, said colleagues in Mbuji-Mayi contacted by radio had confirmed the rebel victory.

"The rebels broadcast on local radio, saying 'We have liberated the town, you have nothing to fear, stay at home'," one said. Another said they had passed through the streets with loudhailers, spreading the same message.
Mining sources Zairean troops looted Mbuji-Mayi and fled west to nearby Kananga in at least 30 vehicles stolen from the state mining concern Miba, which dominates the local economy.

Businessmen in the city told colleagues in Lubumbashi, some 1,000 km (600 miles) to the south, that soldiers had plundered shops of electrical goods as well as the premises of Lebanese diamond dealers.
There was no immediate official word on what would be by far the biggest blow so far to the purse of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko's authorities.

With the potentially rich copper and cobalt mines of Lubumbashi's Shaba province in disrepair, the mainly industrial quality diamonds of neighbouring Kasai province have for several years been Zaire's chief source of foreign income.
Mobutu's opponents say much of the wealth went into the pockets of his officials or diamond smugglers.

The rebels under Laurent Kabila have taken about a quarter of Zaire since ethnic Tutsis rose up on its eastern borders with Rwanda and Burundi last October, sending hundreds of thousands of Hutu refugees fleeing.
They took the jungle city of Kisangani on the huge Zaire river three weeks ago, a strategically important coup that showed Zaire's military was a shambles.
But in economic terms Mbuji-Mayi, taken a day before proposed peace talks in South Africa, is their most significant success.
It was seized four days after the rebels severed its main supply route, south by rail through Lubumbashi to Zambia and South Africa, at the town of Kamina.
Rebels have also advanced a fifth of the way from Kamina towards Lubumbashi, 600 km (350 miles) to the south, reaching the small town of Luena on Friday, mining and expatriate sources said.

Mbuji-Mayi's fall is sure to raise tension in Lubumbashi, which Kabila has vowed to take and which looks likely to be next. There is little to stop him. Most residents say the army will not fight and the city is waiting for Kabila with open arms.
